title: How Christians test and admit their hearers
source_text: Εἰ δ᾿ ἐκεῖνοι οὐκ ἔγκλητοι τοῦτο πράττοντες, ἴδωμεν εἰ μὴ Χριστιανοὶ μᾶλλον καὶ τούτων βέλτιον πλήθη ἐπὶ καλοκἀγαθίαν προκαλοῦνται. οἱ μὲν γὰρ δημοσίᾳ διαλεγόμενοι φιλόσοφοι οὐ φυλοκρινοῦσι τοὺς ἀκούοντας. ἀλλ᾿ ὁ βουλόμενος ἕστηκε καὶ ἀκούει· Χριστιανοὶ δὲ κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν αὐτοῖς προβασανίσαντες τῶν ἀκούειν σφῶν βουλομένων τὰς ψυχὰς καὶ κατ᾿ ἰδίαν αὐτοῖς προεπᾴσαντες, ἐπὰν δοκῶσιν αὐτάρκως οἱ ἀκροαταὶ πρὶν εἰς τὸ κοινὸν εἰσελθεῖν ἐπιδεδωκέναι πρὸς τὸ θέλειν καλῶς βιοῦν, τὸ τηνικάδε αὐτοὺς εἰσάγουσιν, ἰδίᾳ μὲν ποιήσαντες τάγμα τῶν ἄρτι ἀρχομένων καὶ εἰσαγομένων καὶ οὐδέπω τὸ σύμβολον τοῦ ἀποκεκαθάρθαι ἀνειληφότων, ἕτερον δὲ τὸ τῶν κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν παραστησάντων ἑαυτῶν τὴν προαίρεσιν οὐκ ἄλλο τι βούλεσθαι ἢ τὰ Χριστιανοῖς δοκοῦντα· παρ᾿ οἷς εἰσι τινὲς τεταγμένοι πρὸς τὸ φιλοπευστεῖν τοὺς βίους καὶ τὰς ἀγωγὰς τῶν προσιόντων, ἵνα τοὺς μὲν τὰ ἐπίῤῥητα πράττοντας ἀποκωλύσωσιν ἥκειν ἐπὶ τὸν κοινὸν αὐτῶν σύλλογον τοὺς δὲ μὴ τοιούτους ὅλῃ ψυχῇ ἀποδεχόμενοι βελτίους ὁσημέραι κατασκευάζωσιν. οἵα δ᾿ ἐστὶν αὐτοῖς ἀγωγὴ καὶ περὶ ἁμαρτανόντων καὶ μάλιστα τῶν ἀκολασταινόντων, οὓς ἀπε λαύνουσι τοῦ κοινοῦ οἱ κατὰ τὸν Κέλσον παραπλήσιοι τοῖς ἐν ταῖς ἀγοραῖς τὰ ἐπιῤῥητότα (τα) ἐπιδεικνυμένοις. καὶ τὸ μὲν τῶν Πυθαγορείων σεμνὸν διδασκαλεῖον κενοτάφια τῶν ἀποστάντων τῆς σφῶν φιλοσοφίας κατεσκεύαζε. λογιζόμενον νεκροὺς αὐτοὺς γεγονέναι· οὗτοι δὲ ὡς ἀπολωλότας καὶ τεθνηκότας τῷ θεῷ τοὺς ὑπ᾿ ἀσελγείας ἤ τινος ἀτόπου νενικημένους ὡς νεκροὺς πενθοῦσι. καὶ ὡς ἐκ νεκρῶν ἀναστάντας. ἐὰν ἀξιόλογον ἐνδείξωνται μεταβολὴν, χρόνῳ πλείονι τῶν κατ᾿ ἀρχὰς εἰσαγομένων ὕστερόν ποτε προσίενται· εἰς οὐδεμίαν ἀρχὴν καὶ προστασίαν τῆς λεγομένης ἐκκλησίας τοῦ θεοῦ καταλέγοντες τοὺς φθάσαντας μετὰ τὸ προσεληλυθέναι τῷ λόγῳ ἐπταικέναι.
pass_a_gloss: And if those are not blameworthy (ἔγκλητοι) doing this, let us see whether Christians do not rather and better than these summon (προκαλοῦνται) multitudes (πλήθη) to nobility of character (καλοκἀγαθίαν). For the philosophers conversing in public do not sort out by kind (φυλοκρινοῦσι) the hearers, but whoever wishes stands and hears; but Christians, as far as possible for them, having first tested the souls of those wishing to hear them, and having first instructed them privately (κατ' ἰδίαν), when the hearers seem sufficiently (αὐτάρκως), before entering into the common (κοινόν), to have progressed (ἐπιδεδωκέναι) toward wishing to live well (καλῶς βιοῦν), then (τὸ τηνικάδε) bring them in (εἰσάγουσιν), having made separately (ἰδίᾳ) one order (τάγμα) of those just beginning (ἀρχομένων) and being introduced (εἰσαγομένων) and not yet having received (ἀνειληφότων) the token (σύμβολον) of having been cleansed (ἀποκεκαθάρθαι), and another that of those who as far as possible have presented (παραστησάντων) their choice (προαίρεσιν) to want nothing other than the things held (δοκοῦντα) by Christians; among whom some are appointed (τεταγμένοι) to inquire into (φιλοπευστεῖν) the lives (βίους) and conduct (ἀγωγάς) of those approaching, so that those doing disreputable things (ἐπίῤῥητα) they may prevent (ἀποκωλύσωσιν) from coming to their common assembly, but those not such, receiving (ἀποδεχόμενοι) with whole soul, they may make better daily (ὁσημέραι). And of what sort is their discipline (ἀγωγή) also concerning those sinning (ἁμαρτανόντων) and especially those living licentiously, whom they drive from (ἀπελαύνουσι) the community, those who according to Celsus are like those in the market-places displaying the most disreputable things. And the revered (σεμνόν) school (διδασκαλεῖον) of the Pythagoreans used to build cenotaphs (κενοτάφια) of those who had departed (ἀποστάντων) from their philosophy, reckoning (λογιζόμενον) them to have become dead; but these mourn (πενθοῦσι) as dead those overcome (νενικημένους) by licentiousness (ἀσελγείας) or some outrage (ἀτόπου), as lost (ἀπολωλότας) and dead to God. And as risen (ἀναστάντας) from the dead, if they show a noteworthy (ἀξιόλογον) change (μεταβολήν), they admit (προσίενται) them later, after a longer time than those being introduced at the beginning; enrolling (καταλέγοντες) into no office (ἀρχήν) and leadership (προστασίαν) of the so-called church of God those who have already (φθάσαντας) stumbled (ἐπταικέναι) after having come to the word.
pass_b_english: If those men are not to blame for doing this, let us see whether Christians do not summon the crowds to goodness and nobility of character even more, and better, than they do. For the philosophers who converse in public do not sort out their hearers: whoever wishes stands and listens. Christians, on the other hand, first test, as far as they can, the souls of those who wish to hear them, and first instruct them privately; then, when the hearers seem, before entering the common assembly, to have made enough progress toward the will to live well, they bring them in. They form a separate class of those who are just beginning and being introduced and have not yet received the sign of their cleansing, and another of those who have shown, as far as they can, that their purpose is to want nothing other than what Christians hold. Among them certain persons are appointed to inquire into the lives and conduct of those who come forward, so that they may bar from their common assembly those who do disreputable things, while those who are not such they welcome with their whole soul and make better day by day.

And what a discipline they keep toward those who sin, especially the licentious, whom they drive out of the community, these people who, according to Celsus, are like those who put on the most disreputable displays in the market-places! The revered school of the Pythagoreans used to build cenotaphs for those who fell away from their philosophy, reckoning that they had become dead men. But Christians mourn as dead those who have been overcome by licentiousness or some other outrage, as men lost and dead to God. And if they show a change worth noting, they receive them back later, as men risen from the dead, after a longer time than is required of those being introduced at the start; but those who have fallen after coming to the word they do not enroll in any office or position of leadership in what is called the church of God.

choices.choice: 'Instruct privately' renders προεπᾴσαντες, literally 'having first sung (charmed) over them', a metaphor for persuasive teaching; kept plain. ἰδίᾳ μὲν ποιήσαντες τάγμα ... ἕτερον δέ is read as 'forming one class separately ... and another', not as 'privately'. 'The sign of their cleansing' (τὸ σύμβολον τοῦ ἀποκεκαθάρθαι) refers to baptism, but the Greek does not name it, so the English does not either. The two classes are the catechumens and the baptized faithful. The staged text splits ἀπελαύνουσι as 'ἀπε λαύνουσι' (scan artefact) and prints ἐπιῤῥητότα(τα) with Koetschau's supplement; both read as normal. 'Dead to God' may echo Romans 6:10-11 or Luke 15:24, 32 ('was dead and is alive'), but neither is quoted; left uncited. The Pythagorean custom of cenotaphs for apostates is reported elsewhere (Clement, Stromata 5.9.57; Iamblichus, Life of Pythagoras 17.74), not cited inline because Origen names no source.
ἰδίᾳ μὲν ποιήσαντες τάγμα ... ἕτερον δέ: 'They form one class privately' -> 'They form a separate class ... and another'; ἰδίᾳ here sets the two classes apart, it does not mean 'in private'.
Pass A gloss adjusted to match (ἰδίᾳ = separately).
